paragraphs.text: To the people who live beneath them, volcanoes can seem silent for generations. Yet a volcano that appears asleep is rarely completely quiet. Deep beneath the surface, molten rock, or magma, pushes against the surrounding crust, gases escape through cracks, and heated groundwater moves through fractured rock. Each of these processes produces signals that can be detected, provided the right instruments are in place. Over the past century, volcanologists have learned to interpret many of these signals, and their work has saved thousands of lives. Even so, predicting exactly when, or even whether, a restless volcano will erupt remains one of the most stubborn problems in the earth sciences.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The most widely used tool is the seismometer, an instrument that records vibrations in the ground. As magma forces its way upwards, it breaks rock and produces swarms of small earthquakes, most too weak to be felt by humans. Scientists pay particular attention to their depth: a cluster of earthquakes that gradually becomes shallower may indicate that magma is approaching the surface. Some volcanoes also generate a continuous, low humming known as tremor, which is thought to arise when fluids flow through underground channels. Because these signals are so varied, an experienced analyst often needs to examine several days of recordings before deciding whether a change is significant.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: A second approach is to measure the shape of the volcano itself. When magma accumulates in a chamber beneath a mountain, the ground above can swell by centimetres or, occasionally, by metres. Before the 1980 eruption of Mount St Helens in the United States, part of the northern side of the mountain bulged outwards dramatically. Today, deformation is tracked with satellite positioning receivers fixed to the ground, with sensitive tiltmeters that detect tiny changes in slope, and with radar images taken from orbit, which allow scientists to map swelling across an entire region without setting foot on it. Satellite radar has proved especially valuable for remote volcanoes, some of which were found to be inflating even though no one had suspected they were active.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Gases offer further clues. As magma rises, falling pressure allows dissolved gases such as carbon dioxide and sulphur dioxide to escape, much as bubbles appear when a bottle of fizzy drink is opened. Changes in the quantity of these gases, or in the ratio between them, can reveal that fresh magma has arrived from depth. More recently, researchers have begun literally to listen to volcanoes using microphones that record infrasound, sound at frequencies too low for the human ear. Because infrasound can travel hundreds or even thousands of kilometres through the atmosphere, a few well-placed stations can detect explosions at volcanoes where no local instruments exist.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: When these methods are combined, the results can be impressive. In 1991, warnings based on monitoring at Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines allowed authorities to evacuate tens of thousands of people before one of the largest eruptions of the twentieth century. However, such successes depend on knowing what is normal for a particular volcano, and that requires years of continuous observation. A large proportion of the world's potentially active volcanoes have no permanent instruments at all, often because they are in poorer countries or difficult terrain. To address this, engineer Dmitri Saavedra has developed solar-powered seismic sensors that cost a fraction of conventional equipment; he argues that a dense network of cheap instruments may be more useful than a few expensive ones.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The deeper difficulty is that unrest does not always end in an eruption. Magma may rise, stall and cool underground, producing all the warning signs without ever reaching the surface. In a study of historical records from volcanoes on several continents, geophysicist Ngaire Holcombe found that more than half of the well-documented episodes of unrest she examined ended without any eruption. She also found that the length of unrest varied enormously: some volcanoes erupted within days of the first signs, while others remained restless for over a decade before finally erupting or falling quiet. In Holcombe's view, this means that no single threshold, such as a certain number of earthquakes per day, can be applied to every volcano.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: For this reason, many observatories now express forecasts as probabilities rather than firm predictions, and they use alert levels, often shown as colours, to communicate changing risk. This approach is more honest, but it creates its own problems. Officials must decide whether to order evacuations that disrupt lives and businesses, knowing that the volcano may do nothing. Repeated false alarms can lead residents to ignore future warnings, while a delayed decision can be fatal. Some observatories now hold regular public meetings in nearby villages to explain what the alert levels mean. Volcanologists increasingly argue that their task is not only to read the instruments but also to build trust with the communities who must act on what those instruments reveal.
paragraphs.label: G

section.text:
Listening to Volcanoes

A. To the people who live beneath them, volcanoes can seem silent for generations. Yet a volcano that appears asleep is rarely completely quiet. Deep beneath the surface, molten rock, or magma, pushes against the surrounding crust, gases escape through cracks, and heated groundwater moves through fractured rock. Each of these processes produces signals that can be detected, provided the right instruments are in place. Over the past century, volcanologists have learned to interpret many of these signals, and their work has saved thousands of lives. Even so, predicting exactly when, or even whether, a restless volcano will erupt remains one of the most stubborn problems in the earth sciences.

B. The most widely used tool is the seismometer, an instrument that records vibrations in the ground. As magma forces its way upwards, it breaks rock and produces swarms of small earthquakes, most too weak to be felt by humans. Scientists pay particular attention to their depth: a cluster of earthquakes that gradually becomes shallower may indicate that magma is approaching the surface. Some volcanoes also generate a continuous, low humming known as tremor, which is thought to arise when fluids flow through underground channels. Because these signals are so varied, an experienced analyst often needs to examine several days of recordings before deciding whether a change is significant.

C. A second approach is to measure the shape of the volcano itself. When magma accumulates in a chamber beneath a mountain, the ground above can swell by centimetres or, occasionally, by metres. Before the 1980 eruption of Mount St Helens in the United States, part of the northern side of the mountain bulged outwards dramatically. Today, deformation is tracked with satellite positioning receivers fixed to the ground, with sensitive tiltmeters that detect tiny changes in slope, and with radar images taken from orbit, which allow scientists to map swelling across an entire region without setting foot on it. Satellite radar has proved especially valuable for remote volcanoes, some of which were found to be inflating even though no one had suspected they were active.

D. Gases offer further clues. As magma rises, falling pressure allows dissolved gases such as carbon dioxide and sulphur dioxide to escape, much as bubbles appear when a bottle of fizzy drink is opened. Changes in the quantity of these gases, or in the ratio between them, can reveal that fresh magma has arrived from depth. More recently, researchers have begun literally to listen to volcanoes using microphones that record infrasound, sound at frequencies too low for the human ear. Because infrasound can travel hundreds or even thousands of kilometres through the atmosphere, a few well-placed stations can detect explosions at volcanoes where no local instruments exist.

E. When these methods are combined, the results can be impressive. In 1991, warnings based on monitoring at Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines allowed authorities to evacuate tens of thousands of people before one of the largest eruptions of the twentieth century. However, such successes depend on knowing what is normal for a particular volcano, and that requires years of continuous observation. A large proportion of the world's potentially active volcanoes have no permanent instruments at all, often because they are in poorer countries or difficult terrain. To address this, engineer Dmitri Saavedra has developed solar-powered seismic sensors that cost a fraction of conventional equipment; he argues that a dense network of cheap instruments may be more useful than a few expensive ones.

F. The deeper difficulty is that unrest does not always end in an eruption. Magma may rise, stall and cool underground, producing all the warning signs without ever reaching the surface. In a study of historical records from volcanoes on several continents, geophysicist Ngaire Holcombe found that more than half of the well-documented episodes of unrest she examined ended without any eruption. She also found that the length of unrest varied enormously: some volcanoes erupted within days of the first signs, while others remained restless for over a decade before finally erupting or falling quiet. In Holcombe's view, this means that no single threshold, such as a certain number of earthquakes per day, can be applied to every volcano.

G. For this reason, many observatories now express forecasts as probabilities rather than firm predictions, and they use alert levels, often shown as colours, to communicate changing risk. This approach is more honest, but it creates its own problems. Officials must decide whether to order evacuations that disrupt lives and businesses, knowing that the volcano may do nothing. Repeated false alarms can lead residents to ignore future warnings, while a delayed decision can be fatal. Some observatories now hold regular public meetings in nearby villages to explain what the alert levels mean. Volcanologists increasingly argue that their task is not only to read the instruments but also to build trust with the communities who must act on what those instruments reveal.

explanation.uk: В абзаці B сказано, що досвідченому аналітикові можуть знадобитися записи за кілька днів, щоб оцінити зміни. Але комп’ютерні програми в тексті взагалі не згадуються, тому порівняти їхню швидкість неможливо.
